entries.689aa2064f67cc941ed3b9b4f6e5b0caa83407be: <div sID="gen13157" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="140" osisID="Ps.140" sID="Ps.140"/> <div eID="gen13157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13158" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13159" type="x-p"/> This and the four following psalms are much of a piece, and the scope of them the same with many that we met with in the beginning and middle of the book of Psalms, though with but few of late. They were penned by David (as it should seem) when he was persecuted by Saul; one of them is said to be his "prayer when he was in the cave," and it is probable that all the rest were penned about the same time. In this psalm, I. David complains of the malice of his enemies, and prays to God to preserve him from them, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.1-Ps.140.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He encourages himself in God as his God, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.6-Ps.140.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. III. He prays for, and prophesies, the destruction of his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.8-Ps.140.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. IV. He assures all God's afflicted people that their troubles would in due time end well (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.12-Ps.140.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>), with which assurance we must comfort ourselves, and one another, in singing this psalm.
entries.26739674db762ae95a6e6453a5d56fa625238c94: <div eID="gen13159" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13158" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen13160" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Deliver me, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man; <hi type="super">2</hi> Which imagine mischiefs in <hi type="italic">their</hi> heart; continually are they gathered together <hi type="italic">for</hi> war. 3 They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison <hi type="italic">is</hi> under their lips. Selah. <hi type="super">4</hi> Keep me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the violent man; who have purposed to overthrow my goings. <hi type="super">5</hi> The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah. 6 I said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God: hear the voice of my supplications, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O God</hi> the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle. <div eID="gen13160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13161" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic">this,</hi> as in other things, David was a type of Christ, that he suffered before he reigned, was humbled before he was exalted, and that as there were many who loved and valued him, and sought to do him honour, so there were many who hated and envied him, and sought to do him mischief, as appears by these verses, where, <div eID="gen13161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13162" type="x-p"/> I. He gives a character of his enemies, and paints them out in their own colours, as dangerous men, whom he had reason to be afraid of, but wicked men, whom he had no reason to think the righteous God would countenance. There was one that seems to have been the ring-leader of them, whom he calls <hi type="italic">the evil man</hi> and <hi type="italic">the man of violences</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">4</reference>), probably he means Saul. The Chaldee paraphrast (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.9">v. 9</reference>) names both Doeg and Ahithophel; but between them there was a great distance of time. Violent men are evil men. But there were many besides this one who were confederate against David, who are here represented as the genuine offspring and seed of the serpent. For, 1. They are very subtle, crafty to do mischief; they have imagined it (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.2">v. 2</reference>), have laid the scheme with all the art and cunning imaginable. They <hi type="italic">have purposed</hi> and plotted <hi type="italic">to overthrow the goings</hi> of a good man (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">v. 4</reference>), to draw him into sin and trouble, to ruin him by blasting his reputation, crushing his interest, and taking away his life. For this purpose <hi type="italic">they have,</hi> like mighty hunters, <hi type="italic">hidden a snare,</hi> and <hi type="italic">spread a net,</hi> and <hi type="italic">set gins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.5">v. 5</reference>), that their designs against him, being kept undiscovered, might be the more likely to take effect, and he might fall into their hands ere he was aware. Great persecutors have often been great politicians, which has indeed made them the more formidable; but <hi type="italic">the Lord preserves the simple</hi> without all those arts. 2. They are very spiteful, as full of malice as Satan himself: <hi type="italic">They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent,</hi> that infuses his venom with his tongue; and there is so much malignity in all they say that one would think there was nothing <hi type="italic">under their lips</hi> but <hi type="italic">adders' poison,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">v. 3</reference>. With their calumnies, and with their counsels, they aimed to destroy David, but secretly, as a man is stung with a serpent, or a snake in the grass. And they endeavoured likewise to infuse their malice into others, and to make them seven times more the children of hell than themselves. A malignant tongue makes men like the old serpent; and poison in the lips is a certain sign of poison in the heart. 3. They are confederate; they are many of them; but they are all <hi type="italic">gathered together</hi> against me <hi type="italic">for war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.140.2">v. 2</reference>. Those who can agree in nothing else can agree to persecute a good man. Herod and Pilate will unite in this, and in this they resemble Satan, who is not divided against himself, all the devils agreeing in Beelzebub. 4. They are <hi type="italic">proud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.5">v. 5</reference>), conceited of themselves and confident of their success; and herein also they resemble Satan, whose reigning ruining sin was pride. The pride of persecutors, though at present it be the terror, yet may be the encouragement, of the persecuted, for the more haughty they are the faster are they ripening for ruin. <hi type="italic">Pride goes before destruction.</hi> <div eID="gen13162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13163" type="x-p"/> II. He prays to God to keep him from them and from being swallowed up by them: "Lord, <hi type="italic">deliver me, preserve me, keep me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">4</reference>); let them not prevail to take away my life, my reputation, my interest, my comfort, and to prevent my coming to the throne. <hi type="italic">Keep me</hi> from doing as they do, or as they would have me do, or as they promise themselves I shall do." Note, The more malice appears in our enemies against us the more earnest we should be in prayer to God to take us under his protection. In him believers may count upon a security, and may enjoy it and themselves with a holy serenity. Those are safe whom God preserves. If he be for us, who can be against us? <div eID="gen13163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13164" type="x-p"/> III. He triumphs in God, and thereby, in effect, he triumphs over his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.6-Ps.140.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. When his enemies sharpened their tongues against him, did he sharpen his against them? No; <hi type="italic">adders' poison</hi> was <hi type="italic">under their lips,</hi> but grace was poured into his lips, witness what he here said unto the Lord, for to him he looked, to him he directed himself, when he saw himself in so much danger, through the malice of his enemies: and it is well for us that we have a God to go to. He comforted himself, 1. In his interest in God: "<hi type="italic">I said, Thou art my God;</hi> and, if my God, then my shield and mighty protector." In troublous dangerous times it is good to claim relation to God, and by faith to keep hold of him. 2. In his access to God. This comforted him, that he was not only taken into covenant with God, but into communion with him, that he had leave to speak to him, and might expect an answer of peace from him, and could say, with a humble confidence, <hi type="italic">Hear the voice of my supplications, O Lord!</hi> 3. In the assurance he had of help from God and happiness in him: "<hi type="italic">O God the Lord</hi>—<hi type="italic">Jehovah Adonai!</hi> as <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> thou art self-existent and self-sufficient, an infinitely perfect being; as <hi type="italic">Adonai</hi> thou art my stay and support, my ruler and governor, and therefore <hi type="italic">the strength of my salvation,</hi> my strong Saviour; nay, not only my Saviour, but my salvation itself, from whom, in whom, my salvation is; not only a strong Saviour, but the very strength of my salvation, on whom the stress of my hope is laid; all in all, to make me happy, and to preserve me to my happiness." 4. In the experience he had had formerly of God's care of him: <hi type="italic">Thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.</hi> As he pleaded with Saul, that, for the service of his country, he many a time jeoparded his life in the high places of the field, so he pleads with God that, in those services, he had wonderfully protected him, and provided him a better helmet for the securing of his head than Goliath's was: "Lord, thou hast kept me <hi type="italic">in the day of battle</hi> with the Philistines, suffer me not to fall by the treacherous intrigues of false-hearted Israelites." God is as able to preserve his people from secret fraud as from open force; and the experience we have had of his power and care, in dangers of one kind, may encourage us to trust in him and depend upon him in dangers of another nature; for nothing can shorten the Lord's right hand.
entries.01e94aa675295c5544b2ce7808972d5d479090d7: <div eID="gen13164" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Shame and Confusion of Persecutors.</title> <div sID="gen13165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Grant not, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , the desires of the wicked: further not his wicked device; <hi type="italic">lest</hi> they exalt themselves. Selah. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> the head of those that compass me about, let the mischief of their own lips cover them. <hi type="super">10</hi> Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again. <hi type="super">11</hi> Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> I know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will maintain the cause of the afflicted, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the right of the poor. <hi type="super">13</hi> Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence. <div eID="gen13165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13166" type="x-p"/> Here is the believing foresight David had, <div eID="gen13166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13167" type="x-p"/> I. Of the shame and confusion of persecutors. <div eID="gen13167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13168" type="x-p"/> 1. Their disappointment. This he prays for (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">v. 8</reference>), that their lusts might not be gratified, their lust of ambition, envy, and revenge: "<hi type="italic">Grant not, O Lord! the desires of the wicked,</hi> but frustrate them; let them not see the ruin of my interest, which they so earnestly wish to see; but <hi type="italic">hear the voice of my supplications.</hi>" He prays that their projects might not take effect, but be blasted: "<hi type="italic">O further not his wicked device;</hi> let not Providence favour any of his designs, but cross them; suffer <hi type="italic">not his wicked device</hi> to proceed, but chain his wheels, and stop him in the career of his pursuits." Thus we are to pray against the enemies of God's people, that they may not succeed in any of their enterprises. Such was David's prayer against Ahithophel, that God would turn his counsels into foolishness. The plea is, <hi type="italic">lest they exalt themselves,</hi> value themselves upon their success as if it were an evidence that God favoured them. Proud men, when they prosper, are made prouder, grow more impudent against God and insolent against his people, and <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> "Lord, do not prosper them." <div eID="gen13168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13169" type="x-p"/> 2. Their destruction. This he prays for (as we read it); but some choose to read it rather as a prophecy, and the original will bear it. If we take it as a prayer, that proceeds from a spirit of prophecy, which comes all to one. He foretels the ruin, <div eID="gen13169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13170" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of his own enemies: "<hi type="italic">As for those that compass me about,</hi> and seek my ruin," [1.] "<hi type="italic">The mischief of their own lips</hi> shall <hi type="italic">cover</hi> their heads (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.9">v. 9</reference>); the evil they have wished to me shall come upon themselves, their curses shall be blown back into their own faces, and the very designs which they have laid against me shall turn to their own ruin," <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15-Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 15, 16</reference>. Let those that make mischief, by slandering, tale-bearing, misrepresenting their neighbours, and spreading ill-natured characters and stories, dread the consequence of it, and think how sad their condition will be when all the mischief they have been accessory to shall be made to return upon themselves. [2.] The judgments of God shall <hi type="italic">fall upon them,</hi> compared here to <hi type="italic">burning coals,</hi> in allusion to the destruction of Sodom; nay, as in the deluge the waters from above, and those from beneath, met for the drowning of the world, both the windows of heaven were opened and the fountains of the great deep were broken up, so here, to complete the ruin of the enemies of Christ and his kingdom, they shall not only have <hi type="italic">burning coals</hi> cast upon them from above (<reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job xx. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">xxvii. 22</reference>), but they themselves shall <hi type="italic">be cast into the fire</hi> beneath; both heaven and hell, the wrath of God the Judge and the rage of Satan the tormentor, shall concur to make them miserable. And the fire they shall be cast into is not a furnace of fire, out of which perhaps they might escape, but a <hi type="italic">deep pit,</hi> out of which they cannot rise. Tophet is said to be <hi type="italic">deep and large,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen13170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13171" type="x-p"/> (2.) Of all others that are like them, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.11">v. 11</reference>. [1.] Evil speakers must expect to be shaken, for they shall never <hi type="italic">be established in the earth.</hi> What is got by fraud and falsehood, by calumny and unjust accusation, will not prosper, will not last. Wealth gotten by vanity will be diminished. Let not such men as Doeg think to reign long, for his doom will be theirs, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 5</reference>. A lying tongue is but for a moment, but the <hi type="italic">lip of truth shall be established for ever.</hi> [2.] Evil doers must expect to be destroyed: <hi type="italic">Evil shall hunt the violent man,</hi> as the blood-hound hunts the murderer to discover him, as the lion hunts his prey to tear it to pieces. Mischievous men will be brought to light, and brought to ruin; the destruction appointed shall run them down and overthrow them. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners.</hi> <div eID="gen13171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13172" type="x-p"/> II. Here is his foresight of the deliverance and comfort of the persecuted, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.12-Ps.140.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. 1. God will do those justice, in delivering them, who, being wronged, commit themselves to him: "<hi type="italic">I know that the Lord will maintain the</hi> just and injured <hi type="italic">cause of</hi> his <hi type="italic">afflicted</hi> people, and will not suffer might always to prevail against right, though it be but <hi type="italic">the right of the poor,</hi> who have but little that they can pretend a right to." God is, and will be, the patron of oppressed innocence, much more of persecuted piety; those that know him cannot but know this. 2. They will do him justice (if I may so speak), in ascribing the glory of their deliverance to him: "<hi type="italic">Surely the righteous</hi> (who make conscience of rendering to God his due, as well as to men theirs) <hi type="italic">shall give thanks unto thy name</hi> when they find their cause pleaded with jealousy and prosecuted with effect." The closing words, <hi type="italic">The upright shall dwell in thy presence,</hi> denote both God's favour to them ("Thou shalt admit them to dwell in thy presence in grace here, in glory hereafter, and it shall be their safety and happiness") and their duty to God: "They shall attend upon thee as servants that keep in the presence of their masters, both to do them honour and to receive their commands." This is true thanksgiving, even thanksliving; and this use we should make of all our deliverance, we should serve God the more closely and cheerfully.  <chapter eID="Ps.140"/> <div eID="gen13172" type="x-p"/>

entries.669a551c21cd146794ed9730ffd710f9d2400aee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7084"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 140</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.140.1-Ps.140.13">Psa 140:1-13</reference>. The style of this Psalm resembles those of David in the former part of the book, presenting the usual complaint, prayer, and confident hope of relief.</title> <div sID="gen10864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7084"/><hi type="bold">1. evil man--</hi>Which of David's enemies is meant is not important. <div eID="gen10864" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f75b30929ba6bbbe0d561863120adab6c08011b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7085"/><div sID="gen10865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7085"/>2-5. This character of the wicked, and the devices planned against the pious, correspond to <reference osisRef="Ps.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.13">31:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.4">58:4</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen10865" type="x-p"/>
entries.bad1182864374701ec3b635756de3fb44f1dc724: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7088"/><div sID="gen10868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7088"/>6. (Compare Psa 5:1-12; 16:2). <div eID="gen10868" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a64afb7c82bdabfa6ddc8ef8764c7c2c87d0697: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7089"/><div sID="gen10869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7089"/><hi type="bold">7. day of battle--</hi>literally, "of armor," that is, when using it. <div eID="gen10869" type="x-p"/>
entries.59105c09eb5b0c69637ed897d4e51f48b161ac5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7090"/><div sID="gen10870" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7090"/>8. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12">Psa 37:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.7">66:7</reference>).<div eID="gen10870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest they exalt themselves--</hi>or, they will be exalted if permitted to prosper. <div eID="gen10871" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a68cb956707ad907661bb8a2157cd12caea1015: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7091"/><div sID="gen10872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7091"/>9. Contrasts his head covered by God (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.7">Psa 140:7</reference>) with theirs, or (as "head" may be used for "persons") with them, covered with the results of their wicked deeds (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>). <div eID="gen10872" type="x-p"/>
entries.665041aedf5d0a9bf49a0164e75560b29016fc56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7092"/><div sID="gen10873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7092"/>10. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.120.4">120:4</reference>).<div eID="gen10873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast into the fire; into deep pits--</hi>figures for utter destruction. <div eID="gen10874" type="x-p"/>
entries.40389a5804f46edde9ad76b7a4e57ab00e8d37a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7093"/><div sID="gen10875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7093"/><hi type="bold">11. an evil speaker--</hi>or, "slanderer" will not be tolerated (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference>). The last clause may be translated: "an evil (man) He (God) shall hunt," &c. <div eID="gen10875" type="x-p"/>
entries.e07b1bc74864dd805cb924b66af60eb56d05ea92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7094"/><div sID="gen10876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7094"/>12. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.4">Psa 9:4</reference>). <div eID="gen10876" type="x-p"/>
entries.a62403b484e757a000a9ef867f11df1710e28772: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7095"/><div sID="gen10877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7095"/>13. After all changes, the righteous shall have cause for praise. Such<div eID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall dwell--</hi>shall sit securely, under God's protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.6">Psa 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.41.12">41:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.140"/>

entries.b94cc9a80e625e80e37cd59bb18d578c204eb11e: <div eID="gen23360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23363" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.140.1-Psa.140.6">Psa 140:1-6</reference>; returns thanks for help, <reference osisRef="Psa.140.7">Psa 140:7</reference>; describes his enemies, and prays farther against them, <reference osisRef="Psa.140.8-Psa.140.11">Psa 140:8-11</reference>. His confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.140.12">Psa 140:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.140.13">Psa 140:13</reference>. <div eID="gen23363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23364" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew, and all the Versions, attribute this Psalm to David; and it is supposed to contain his complaint when persecuted by Saul. The Syriac determines it to the time when Saul endeavored to transfix David with his spear. <div eID="gen23364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23366" type="x-p"/> From the evil man - Saul, who was full of envy, jealousy, and cruelty against David, to whom both himself and his kingdom were under the highest obligations, endeavored by every means to destroy him.
entries.a8f4f29a09efba05b8a46f211aaba523dacada37: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23367" type="x-p"/> They gathered together - He and his courtiers form plots and cabals against my life.
entries.60917d15675ccdc7137ffed502655a0a94c70180: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23368" type="x-p"/> They have sharpened their tongues - They employ their time in forging lies and calumnies against me; and those of the most virulent nature.
entries.7fa010001f95c0f2232a219c4a135dda5bb4d25a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23369" type="x-p"/> Preserve me from the violent man - Saul again; who was as headstrong and violent in all his measures, as he was cruel, and inflexibly bent on the destruction of David.
entries.f2cc4e114418d54c0947448add587dae12b7a046: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23370" type="x-p"/> Have hid a snare for me - They hunted David as they would a dangerous wild beast: one while striving to pierce him with the spear; another to entangle him in their snares, so as to take and sacrifice him before the people, on pretense of his being an enemy to the state. <div eID="gen23370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23371" type="x-p"/> Selah - This is the truth.
entries.e3e0d6fc4535681bbc7a6283825e8afc4e3e19c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23372" type="x-p"/> Thou hast covered my head - Not only when I fought with the proud blaspheming Philistine; but in the various attempts made against my life by my sworn enemies.
entries.cdc0bcba87474b3d1e9f391af02f2cf08be14db7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23373" type="x-p"/> Further not his wicked device - He knew his enemies still desired his death, and were plotting to accomplish it; and here he prays that God may disappoint and confound them. The Chaldee understands this of Doeg.
entries.e70ec366d331f0f1af564a954c635dc348d44300: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23374" type="x-p"/> Let burning coals - The Chaldee considers this as spoken against Ahithophel, who was head of a conspiracy against David; and translates this verse thus: "Let coals from heaven fall upon them, precipitate them into the fire of hell, and into miry pits, from which they shall not have a resurrection to eternal life." This is a proof that the Jews did believe in a resurrection of the body, and an eternal life for that body, in the case of the righteous.
entries.28f73f019409bb42279a5e0b304ba4531bd75037: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23375" type="x-p"/> Let not an evil speaker be established - איש לשון ish lashon, "a man of tongue." There is much force in the rendering of this clause in the Chaldee גבר דמשתעי לישן תליתי gebar demishtai lishan telithai, "The man of detraction, or inflammation, with the three-forked tongue." He whose tongue is set on fire from hell; the tale-bearer, slanderer, and dealer in scandal: with the three-forked tongue; wounding three at once: his neiphbour whom he slanders; the person who receives the slander; and himself who deals in it. What a just description of a character which God, angels, and good men must detest! Let not such a one be established in the land; let him be unmasked; let no person trust him; and let all join together to hoot him out of society. "He shall be hunted by the angel of death, and thrust into hell." - Chaldee.
entries.922af5eeee8100fade7a11f1585ac4fd44d5bfd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23376" type="x-p"/> The cause of the afflicted - Every person who is persecuted for righteousness' sake has God for his peculiar help and refuge; and the persecutor has the same God for his especial enemy.
entries.59d9f118999fcf76b62f3da720d76031f799f7e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23377" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall give thanks - For thou wilt support and deliver him. <div eID="gen23377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23378" type="x-p"/> The upright shall dwell in thy presence - Shall be admitted to the most intimate intercourse with God. <div eID="gen23378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23379" type="x-p"/> The persecuted have ever been dear to God Almighty; and the martyrs were, in an especial manner, his delight; and in proportion as he loved those, so must he hate and detest these.  <chapter eID="Ps.140"/> <div eID="gen23379" type="x-p"/>

entries.7d86be9de135f041acbf042b54d7203f318456a7: <div eID="gen10286" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Suppliant Cry of One Who Is Utterly Undone</title> <div sID="gen10287" type="x-p"/> The ירוּם of the personal cry with which David opens <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference> harmonizes with כּרם of the general lament which he introduces into <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference>; and for this reason the collector has coupled these two Psalms together. Hitzig assigns <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference> to the time when Saul posted watchers to hunt David from place to place, and when, having been long and unceasingly persecuted, David dared to cherish a hope of escaping death only by indefatigable vigilance and endurance. Perhaps this view is correct. The Psalm consists of three strophes, or if it be preferred, three groups of decreasing magnitude. A long deep sigh is followed, as from a relieved breast, by an already much more gentle and half calm prayer; and this again by the believing joy which anticipates the certainty of being answered. This song as it were casts up constantly lessening waves, until it becomes still as the sea when smooth as a mirror, and the only motion discernible at last is that of the joyous ripple of calm repose.
entries.10840c703fdb4ee0825323713ddde98958222dfb: <reference osisRef="Ps.140.1-Ps.140.3">Psa 140:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10288" type="x-p"/> The assimilation of the <hi type="italic">Nun</hi> of the verb נצר is given up, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.7">Psa 78:7</reference>, and frequently, in order to make the form more full-toned. The relative clause shows that אישׁ חמסים is not intended to be understood exclusively of one person. בּלב strengthens the notion of that which is deeply concealed and premeditated. It is doubtful whether יגוּרוּ signifies to form into troops or to stir up. But from the fact that גּוּר in <reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.15">Isa 54:15</reference>, signifies not <hi type="italic">congregare</hi> but <hi type="italic">se congregare</hi>, it is to be inferred that גּוּר in the passage before us, like גּרה (or התגּרה in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.9">Deu 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.24">Deu 2:24</reference>), in Syriac and Targumic גּרג, signifies <hi type="italic">concitare</hi>, to excite (cf. שׂוּר together with שׂרה, Hos 12:4.). In <reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">Psa 140:4</reference> the Psalm coincides with <reference osisRef="Ps.64.4">Psa 64:4</reference>; Psa 58:5. They sharpen their tongue, so that it inflicts a fatal sting like the tongue of a serpent, and under their lips, shooting out from thence, is the poison of the adder (cf. Sol 4:11). עכשׁוּב is a ἅπαξ λεγομ. not from כּשׁב (<hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi>, p. 207), but from עכשׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ks</hi> and <hi type="italic">‛kš</hi>, root <hi type="italic">‛k</hi> (vid., Fleischer on <reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference>, עכּבישׁ), both of which have the significations of bending, turning, and coiling after the manner of a serpent; the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is an organic addition modifying the meaning of the root.<note placement="foot">According to the original Lexicons Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ks</hi> signifies to bend one’s self, to wriggle, to creep sideways like the roots of the vine, in the V form to move one’s self like an adder (according to the <hi type="italic">Ḳamûs</hi>) and to walk like a drunken man (according to <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi>); but Arab. <hi type="italic">‛kš</hi> signifies to be intertwined, knit or closely united together, said of hairs and of the branches of trees, in the V form to fight hand to hand and to get in among the crowd. The root is apparently expanded into עכשׁוב by an added <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> which serves as a notional speciality, as in Arab. <hi type="italic">‛rqûb</hi> the convex bend of the steep side of a rock, or in the case of the knee of the hind-legs of animals, and in Arab. <hi type="italic">charnûb</hi> (in the dialect of the country along the coast of Palestine, where the tree is plentiful, in Neshwân <hi type="italic">churnûb</hi>), the horn-like curved pod of the carob-tree (<hi type="italic">Ceratonia Siliqua</hi>), syncopated Arab. <hi type="italic">charrûb</hi>, <hi type="italic">charrûb</hi> (not <hi type="italic">charûb</hi>), from Arab. <hi type="italic">charn</hi>, cogn. <hi type="italic">qarn</hi>, a horn, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">chrnâyt</hi>, the beak of a bird of prey, Arab. <hi type="italic">chrnûq</hi>, the stork [<hi type="italic">vid</hi>. on Psa 104:17], Arab. <hi type="italic">chrnı̂n</hi>, the rhinoceros [<hi type="italic">vid</hi>. on Psa 29:6], Arab. <hi type="italic">chrnuı̂t</hi>, the unicorn [<hi type="italic">vid. ibid.</hi>]<hi type="italic">.</hi> - Wetzstein.</note>
entries.606a23b3cffad9835af70fc121697def50bced9a: <reference osisRef="Ps.140.4-Ps.140.5">Psa 140:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen10288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10289" type="x-p"/> The course of this second strophe is exactly parallel with the first. The perfects describe their conduct hitherto, as a comparison of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference></hi> with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference></hi> shows. פּעמים is poetically equivalent to רגלים, and signifies both the foot that steps (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.5">Psa 57:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.11">Psa 58:11</reference>) and the step that is made by the foot (Ps 85:14; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.133">Psa 119:133</reference>), and here the two senses are undistinguishable. They are called גּאים on account of the inordinate ambition that infatuates them. The metaphors taken from the life of the hunter (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.9">Psa 141:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>) are here brought together as it were into a body of synonyms. The meaning of ליד־מעגּל becomes explicable from <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>; ליד, at hand, is equivalent to “immediately beside” (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.17">1Ch 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.24">Neh 11:24</reference>). Close by the path along which he has to pass, lie gins ready to spring together and ensnare him when he appears.
entries.b16086bc34e7c629ead2bb0251a393c6c6aef441: <reference osisRef="Ps.140.6-Ps.140.8">Psa 140:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen10289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10290" type="x-p"/> Such is the conduct of his enemies; he, however, prays to his God and gets his weapons from beside Him. The day of equipment is the day of the crisis when the battle is fought in full array. The perfect סכּותה states what will then take place on the part of God: He protects the head of His anointed against the deadly blow. Both <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference></hi> point to the helmet as being מעוז ראשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>; cf. the expression “the helmet of salvation” in Isa 59:17. Beside מאויּי, from the ἅπ. λεγ. מאוה, there is also the reading מאויי, which Abulwalîd found in his Jerusalem codex (in Saragossa). The regular form would be מאוי, and the boldly irregular <hi type="italic">ma'awajjê</hi> follows the example of מחשׁכּי, מחמדּי, and the like, in a manner that is without example elsewhere. זממז for מזמּתו is also a hapaxlegomenon; according to Gesenius the principal form is זמם, but surely ore correctly זמם (like קרב), which in Aramaic signifies a bridle, and here a plan, device. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. חפיק (root פק, whence נפק, Arab. <hi type="italic">nfq</hi>) signifies <hi type="italic">educere</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">reportare</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.13">Pro 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.35">Pro 8:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">Pro 18:22</reference>, and of <hi type="italic">porrigere</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.13">Psa 144:13</reference>, Isa 58:10. A reaching forth of the plan is equivalent to the reaching forth of that which is projected. The choice of the words used in this Psalm coincides here, as already in מעגּל, with Proverbs and Isaiah. The future ירוּמוּ expresses the consequence (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>) against which the poet wishes to guard.
entries.ee37bbff9a3483cf0f96b723fdd174a05394ac46: <reference osisRef="Ps.140.9-Ps.140.11">Psa 140:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen10290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10291" type="x-p"/> The strophic symmetry is now at an end. The longer the poet lingers over the contemplation of the rebels the more lofty and dignified does his language become, the more particular the choice of the expressions, and the more difficult and unmanageable the construction. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הסב signifies, causatively, to cause to go round about (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">Exo 13:18</reference>), and to raise round about (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.6">2Ch 14:6</reference>); here, after <reference osisRef="Josh.6.11">Jos 6:11</reference>, where with an accusative following it signifies to go round about: to make the circuit of anything, as enemies who surround a city on all sides and seek the most favourable point for assault; מסבּי from the participle מסב. Even when derived from the substantive מסב (Hupfeld), “my surroundings” is equivalent to איבי סביבותי in Psa 27:6. Hitzig, on the other hand, renders it: the head of my slanderers, from סבב, to go round about, Arabic to tell tales of any one, defame; but the Arabic <hi type="italic">sbb , fut. u</hi>, to abuse, the IV form (<hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>) of which moreover is not used either in the ancient or in the modern language, has nothing to do with the Hebrew סבב, but signifies originally to cut off round about, then to clip (injure) any one’s honour and good name.<note placement="foot">The lexicographer <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi> says, i. 279 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - sbb 'l   - šatm w- qı̂l an aṣl 'l - sbb 'l - qaṭ‛ ṯm ṣâr 'l   - štm</hi>, “<hi type="italic">sebb</hi> is to abuse; still, the more original signification of cutting off is said to lie at the foundation of this signification.” That Arab. <hi type="italic">qṭ‛</hi> is synonymous with it, e.g., Arab. <hi type="italic">lı̂štqt‛fı̂nâ</hi>, why dost thou cut into us? i.e., why dost thou insult our honour? - Wetzstein.</note> <div eID="gen10291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10292" type="x-p"/> The fact that the enemies who surround the psalmist on every side are just such calumniators, is intimated here in the word שׂפתימו. He wishes that the trouble which the enemies’ slanderous lips occasion him may fall back upon their own head. ראשׁ is head in the first and literal sense according to <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>; and יכסּימו (with the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of the groundform kcy, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.26">Deu 32:26</reference>; 1Ki 20:35; <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> יכסּוּמו,<note placement="foot">Which is favoured by <reference osisRef="Exod.15.5">Exo 15:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">jechasjûmû</hi> with <hi type="italic">mû</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">mô</hi>, which is otherwise without example.</note> after the attractional schema, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference>, and frequently; cf. on the masculine form, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference>) refers back to ראשׁ, which is meant of the heads of all persons individually. In <reference osisRef="Ps.140.11">Psa 140:11</reference> ימיטוּ (with an indefinite subject of the higher punitive powers, Ges. §137, note), in the signification to cause to descend, has a support in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.4">Psa 55:4</reference>, whereas the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נמוט, <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ימּט, which is preferred by the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, in the signification to be made to descend, is contrary to the usage of the language. The ἅπ. λεγ. מהמרות has been combined by Parchon and others with the Arabic <hi type="italic">hmr</hi>, which, together with other significations (to strike, stamp, cast down, and the like), also has the signification to flow (whence e.g., in the Koran, <hi type="italic">mâ' munhamir</hi>, flowing water). “Fire” and “water” are emblems of perils that cannot be escaped, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>, and the mention of fire is therefore appropriately succeeded by places of flowing water, pits of water. The signification “pits” is attested by the Targum, Symmachus, Jerome, and the quotation in Kimchi: “first of all they buried them in מהמורות; when the flesh was consumed they collected the bones and buried them in coffins.” On בּל־יקוּמוּ cf. Isa 26:14. Like <reference osisRef="Ps.140.10-Ps.140.11">Psa 140:10-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.12">Psa 140:12</reference> is also not to be taken as a general maxim, but as expressing a wish in accordance with the excited tone of this strophe. אישׁ לשׁון is not a great talker, i.e., boaster, but an idle talker, i.e., slanderer (lxx ἀνὴρ γλωσσώδης, cf. Sir. 8:4). According to the accents, אישׁ חמס רע is the parallel; but what would be the object of this designation of violence as worse or more malignant? With Sommer, Olshausen, and others, we take רע as the subject to יצוּדנּוּ: let evil, i.e., the punishment which arises out of evil, hunt him; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.21">Pro 13:21</reference>, חטּאים תּרדּף רעה, and the opposite in Psa 23:6. It would have to be accented, according to this our construction of the words, אישׁ חמס רע יצודני למדחפת. The ἅπ. λεγ. למדחפת we do not render, with Hengstenberg, Olshausen, and others: push upon push, with repeated pushes, which, to say nothing more, is not suited to the figure of hunting, but, since דּחף always has the signification of precipitate hastening: by hastenings, that is to say, forced marches.
entries.7e322c832622d57095eb81d8545a01646b028718: <reference osisRef="Ps.140.12-Ps.140.13">Psa 140:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen10292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10293" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.140.13">Psa 140:13</reference> the mood and language now again become cheerful, the rage has spent itself; therefore the style and tone are now changed, and the Psalm trips along merrily as it were to the close. With reference to ידעת for ידעתי (as in <reference osisRef="Job.42.2">Job 42:2</reference>), vid., Psa 16:2. That which David in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference> confidently expects on his own behalf is here generalized into the certain prospect of the triumph of the good cause in the person of all its representatives at that time oppressed. אך, like ידעתּי, is an expression of certainty. After seeming abandonment God again makes Himself known to His own, and those whom they wanted to sweep away out of the land of the living have an ever sure dwelling-place with His joyful countenance (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.140"/> <div eID="gen10293" type="x-p"/>

entries.7b887ea347d8f797054cd4010e670db8e1d4fb07:
PSALM 140
David complains of the implacable cruelty of his enemies, and of their treachery and rancorous calumnies. In the close, having besought God’s help, and expressing his persuasion of obtaining his layout, he comforts himself with the hope of deliverance, and just vengeance being executed upon his enemies.
To the chief Musician — A Psalm of David.
Psalm 140:1-5
1. Deliver me, O Jehovah! from the evil man, (homo,) preserve me from the man (vir)
“The word ‘man’ in these two lines is expressed in the first by אדם (homo,) in the second by איש (vir.)” — Jebb’s Translation of the Psalms, etc., volume 1.
of injuries. 2. Who imagine mischiefs in their heart; daily they congregate for war. 3. They have sharpened their tongue like a serpent:
Mant translates —
“The serpent’s brandished tongue is theirs.”
“The verb,” says he, “here rendered ‘brandished,’ signifies either ‘to whet, sharpen,’ which is performed by reiterated motion or friction, or to ‘vibrate.’ In either case the metaphor, as applied to a wicked tongue, is beautiful and appropriate. I have preferred the latter as affording a more poetical image. See Parkhurst on שנן, 3.” In illustration of this figure Kimchi observes, that “the serpent when it comes to bite will open its mouth, and will hiss, and move its tongue here and there as if it would make it sharp as a barber’s razor.”
the poison of an asp
The original word עכשוב, achshub, rendered “asp,” is to be found in Scripture only in this place; and though it evidently denotes some of the serpent tribe, it is not so easy to determine the particular species intended. In our English Bible it is translated “adder,” and as the word is derived from an Arabic verb, which signifies to coil up, or bend back, it has been said that this act perfectly corresponds with the nature of the adder, which in preparing to strike contracts itself into a spiral form, and raises its horrid head from the middle of the orb; and which also assumes the same form when it goes to sleep, coiling its body into a number of circles, with its head in the center. — (Paxton’s Illustrations of Scripture, vol. i. p. 428.) But the same action is common to most serpents; and this name may, therefore have reference to no particular species. Some, however, contend that it is another name for the pethem, or asp mentioned in Job 20:14, the venom of which is so deadly as to be incurable and followed by speedy death, unless the wounded part is amputated. Such seems to have been the opinion of the LXX., as they render it by ασπις, in which they are followed by the Vulgate and by the Apostle Paul, who quotes this text in Romans 3:13. Calvin here adopts the word sanctioned by these authorities.
“As to the poison, it will be observed, that in the venomous serpents there is a gland under the eye secreting the poisonous matter which is conveyed in a small tube or canal to the end of a fang which lies concealed at the roof of the mouth. This fang is moveable at the pleasure of the serpent, and is protruded when it is about to strike at an antagonist. The situation of this poison, which is in a manner behind the upper lip, gives great propriety to the expression — ‘Adders’ poison is under their lips.’ The usage of the Hebrew language, renders it by no means improbable that the fang itself is called לשון, lashon, ‘a tongue,’ in the present text; and a serpent might be said to sharpen its tongue, when in preparing to strike it protruded its fangs. We do not see any explanation by which a more consistent meaning may be extracted from the expression here employed.” — Illustrated Commentary upon the Bible.
is under their lips. Selah 4. Keep us, O Jehovah! from the hands of the wicked: preserve me from the man of injuries, who plot to overthrow my goings. 5. The proud have set a snare for me, and have spread a net with cords: by the way side they have set gins for me.
The imagery in this verse is borrowed from the practices of hunters and fowlers in the eastern regions of the world, who are accustomed to take and destroy the ferocious beasts and the larger species of birds by a variety of ingenious snares and devices. It is a curious circumstance, as noticed by Thevenot, that artifices of this kind are literally employed against men as well as against birds and wild beasts by some of the Orientals. “The cunningest robbers in the world,” says he, as quoted by Mant, “are in this country. They use a certain slip, with a running noose, which they cast with so much slight about a man’s neck when they are within reach of him, that they never fail, so that they strangle him in a trice.”
Selah
 
To the chief Musician, etc. I cannot bring myself to restrict this Psalm to Doeg, as the great body of interpreters do, for the context will clearly show that it speaks of Saul, and of the counselors who ceased not to inflame the king — himself sufficiently incensed against the life of one who was a saint of God. Being as he was a figure of Christ, we need not wonder that the agents of the devil directed so much of their rage against him. And this is the reason why he animadverts so sharply upon their rancor and treachery.
The terms wicked and violent men denote their unwarranted attempts at his destruction without provocation given. He therefore commends his cause to God, as having studied peace with them, as never having injured them, but being the innocent object of their unjust persecution. The same rule must be observed by us all, as it is against violence and wickedness that the help of God is extended. David is not Multiplying mere terms of reproach as men do in their personal disputes, but conciliating God’s favor by supplying a proof of his innocence, for he must always be upon the side of good and peaceable men.

entries.f05c43749c19111dad34738ea8341ace7b4590a2:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="140" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:514" />
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXL.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm was composed by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> upon occasion of those slanderous and reproachful speeches and treacherous deal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had from his enemies, in <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> time, of which we have an account in the history.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 DEliver, me, O LORD, from the evil man <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Doeg</ns0:hi> or some other malicious enemy, or rather enemies: the word <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> being taken collectively for <ns0:hi>men,</ns0:hi> as appears from the next verse, where he speaks of this man in the Plural number.</ns0:note>: preserve me from the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> man of violences.</ns0:note> violent man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Which imagine mischiefs in <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> heart: continually are they gathered together for war <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To execute those bloody enterprises which they had devised in the first clause of this verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 They have sharpned their tongues <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Their malicious hearts stirred up their tongues to utter vile slanders against me.</ns0:note> like a serpent <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either whetting their tongues as serpents are said to whet theirs when they are about to bite: or rather, using words as sharp and piercing as the sting of a serpent.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 58. 4<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Rom. 3. 13.</ns0:note> adders poison <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> under their lips.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked, preserve me from the violent man, who have purposed <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Whose design and full resolution it is, if thou dost not prevent it.</ns0:note> to overthrow my goings <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>eet</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>footsteps, i. e.</ns0:hi> to throw me down to the ground, to defeat all my hopes and counsels, and bring me to ruine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 35. 7. & 57. 6. & 141. 9. Jer. 18. 22.</ns0:note> The proud <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">My in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>olent enemies who despise me for my meanness, and exalt themselves against thee.</ns0:note> have hid a snare for me, and cords, they have spread a net by the way <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> hand.</ns0:note> side <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In which I used to walk.</ns0:note>: they have set grins for me. Selah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 I said unto the LORD, Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> my God: hear the voice of my supplications, O LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 O GOD the Lord, the strength of my sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation; thou hast covered my head <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">With thy powerful protection as with an helmet or shield.</ns0:note> in the day of battel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked, further not his wicked device <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which is to destroy me.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>let them not</ns0:hi> be <ns0:hi>exalted.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 32. 27.</ns0:note> lest they exalt themselves <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not onely against me, but against thee also, as if by their power and policy they had frustrated thy design and promise made to me.</ns0:note>. Selah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:hi>As for</ns0:hi> the head <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>beads,</ns0:hi> the Singular number put for the Plural, as is frequent. By which he understands either, 1. their poli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tick heads, their chiefs or ring-leaders, who were most ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />licious, and by whom all the rest were supported and stirred<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> up: or, 2. their proper and natural heads, as this word is<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> used <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. and this covering of their heads here is opposed to that covering of <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> head there.</ns0:note> of those that compass me about, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 7. 16. & 94. 23. Prov. 12. 13. & 18. 7.</ns0:note> let the mischief of their own lips cover them <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Let the mischief which by their calumnies they design against me, fall upon themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 11. 6.</ns0:note> Let burning coals <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Divine vengeance, which is compared to coals of fire, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 18. 12. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> fall upon them, let them be cast into the fire: into deep pits, that they rise not up again <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either to my danger, or to their own comfort.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Let not <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a man of tongue.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>an evil speaker, a wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed man of vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence be esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished in the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>arth: let him be hunted to</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>overthrow.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> an evil speaker <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Such as slander me and other innocent persons, to ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />asperate Princes against us.</ns0:note> be establish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in the earth: evil <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either the evil of punishment, or, which comes to the same thing, the evil of sin, their own wickedness, which shall recoil upon themselves.</ns0:note> shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 I know <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Both by Gods word which hath promised it, and by my own experience of it in the course of Gods providence.</ns0:note> that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the right of the poor.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy Name <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Shall have occasion to praise thee for their deliverance.</ns0:note>, the upright shall dwell in thy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Shall constantly enjoy thy gracious and powerful presence and assistance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>

Poole.heading: PSAL. CXL. To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David.
